Tech Report: A Study of 50,000 Children Reveals the Real Impact of Daily Iron Pills

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major scientific review involving more than 50,000 children and adolescents reveals that daily iron supplementation can significantly reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia.
  • It has been revealed that A daily iron supplement can substantially reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia in children and teenagers, but it does not appear to improve growth or protect against common illnesses.
  • Led by researchers at Cornell University’s Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, the review examined daily iron supplements taken alone or combined with folic acid and other vitamins and minerals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major scientific review involving more than 50,000 children and adolescents reveals that daily iron supplementation can significantly reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia.

It has been revealed that A daily iron supplement can substantially reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia in children and teenagers, but it does not appear to improve growth or protect against common illnesses. These findings come from a major Cochrane review of 114 studies involving more than 50,000 participants.

Led by researchers at Cornell University’s Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, the review examined daily iron supplements taken alone or combined with folic acid and other vitamins and minerals. Many of the studies were conducted in Asia and involved children younger than five.

According to recent reports, the strongest evidence demonstrated that iron alone probably reduces the risk of iron deficiency anemia compared with receiving no treatment or a placebo. Combining iron with folic acid probably offers similar protection, although that conclusion was based on just one study. Supplements containing iron alongside other vitamins and minerals may also help. Evidence suggests that iron supplementation can reduce anemia and iron deficiency more broadly, but confidence in several findings remains limited.

Sources indicate that iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the lungs throughout the body. When iron levels become too low, the body cannot produce enough healthy hemoglobin, potentially leading to iron deficiency anemia.

Industry observers note that “Iron deficiency remains one of the most common nutritional problems affecting children worldwide,” claims first author Dr Kripa Rajagopalan. “Our review reveals that daily iron supplements do what they are meant to do, which is reduce iron deficiency anemia, without any measurable impact on the common illnesses parents and health workers worry about.”.

Although iron supplements helped prevent iron deficiency anemia, the researchers found no improvement in children’s height or weight relative to others of the same age and sex. Iron alone also had no measurable effect on the occurrence of cough, fever, or respiratory illness.

Adding folic acid to iron made little to no difference in rates of diarrhea or respiratory illness. Results for other supplement combinations were less conclusive, with evidence ranging from moderate to very low certainty.

Daily iron supplementation may cause stool discoloration, but iron alone appears to have little or no effect on vomiting or diarrhea. Its relationship with constipation remains uncertain. When iron was included in supplements containing other vitamins and minerals, vomiting was probably more common than with otherwise identical supplements that lacked iron.

It has been revealed that “While the evidence base supports the use of daily iron supplements where needed, some adverse effects do occur. Stool discoloration and, in some formulations, vomiting were more common with iron, and the certainty of evidence for several outcomes, including anemia and iron deficiency themselves, was low or very low,” explains senior author Dr Saurabh Mehta.

Uncertainty about longer-term outcomes has persisted for years. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, last updated in 2016, identified gaps in evidence concerning the long-term effects of iron supplementation in children. The new review brings together a much larger body of research, although the strength of the evidence still varies across outcomes.

According to recent reports, anemia affects an estimated 874 million children and women worldwide. Young children face a particularly heavy burden, with approximately 40% of children younger than five affected in 2019. Iron deficiency accounts for roughly half of these cases.

Preventing anemia is a central objective of the global health strategy for women, children, and adolescents through 2030. Iron supplementation is already widely used to prevent and treat anemia, particularly among adolescents and women in populations where iron deficiency is common.

Recent findings suggest that “These findings give decision-makers a stronger evidence base for guidance on iron supplementation in children and adolescents,” says co-author Dr Julia L. Finkelstein. “The data supports continued use of iron supplementation where iron deficiency is a concern.”.

The researchers caution that their findings do not justify giving every child or adolescent a daily iron tablet. Decisions about supplementation should account for individual nutritional needs, local rates of iron deficiency and anemia, and the specific supplement formulation being used.

Reference: “Daily iron supplementation for prevention or treatment of iron‐deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and adolescents” by Kripa Rajagopalan, Laura Hackl, Juan Pablo Peña-Rosas, Maria Nieves Garcia-Casal, Mochammad Rizal, Neel H Mehta, Michael Roudik, Saiful Islam, Meghan M Trumbull-Kennedy, Nabila Reem Khondakar, Juan VA Franco, Julia L Finkelstein and Saurabh Mehta, 17 November 2026, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD013227.pub2.

  • While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

Sources indicate that the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Recent findings suggest that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Recent findings suggest that every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

Industry observers note that I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody states they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

According to recent reports, while more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

In a recent development, this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated promptly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be mentioned is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Scientists X-Ray a Narwhal Tusk and Discover Something Extraordinary

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists are uncovering the secrets of narwhal tusks, revealing an unusual internal structure and new possibilities for studying decades of environmental change in the Arctic.
  • It has been revealed that in the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns.
  • Unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses or the incisors of beavers, the male narwhal’s tusk grows forward in an elegant spiral.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists are uncovering the secrets of narwhal tusks, revealing an unusual internal structure and new possibilities for studying decades of environmental change in the Arctic.

It has been revealed that in the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns. The extraordinary royal treasure came from an expedition he sent to Greenland, where the king knew the precious horns could be traced to a very real animal. It lived in Arctic waters, had fins instead of hooves, and was known as the narwhal. The expedition was a success, bringing the Danish ruler a throne that became a symbol of prestige and power across Europe. Yet the legendary horn was not a horn at all. It was a tooth.

And what a peculiar tooth it is. Unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses or the incisors of beavers, the male narwhal’s tusk grows forward in an elegant spiral. Usually, it is the left upper canine that extends through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it reaches lengths of up to two meters (6.6 feet), sometimes half the animal’s body length.

Sources indicate that that unusual shape has fascinated scientists for years. Now, an international research team has uncovered something remarkable inside the tusk. Its microscopic building blocks form two intertwined spirals that twist in opposite directions, creating a structure that helps the enormous tooth withstand mechanical stress. The findings, published in Nature Communications, offer a fresh explanation for the anatomy behind one of nature’s most recognizable features.

For all their fame, narwhal tusks still hold plenty of mysteries. Scientists do not know exactly how the animals use them, although evidence suggests they play an notable role in mate selection and social interaction. Narwhals have occasionally been observed engaging in playful tusk duels, further supporting a possible connection to reproduction and social behavior. The tusks also continue growing throughout the animal’s life and can themselves reach 70 years of age.

It has been revealed that understanding how such a long, spiraling tooth remains strong requires looking far beneath its surface. “Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth,” says Marianne Liebi, a researcher at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) and co-author of the study.

Most of the tusk consists of dentine, the same material that forms the core of human teeth. A thinner outer layer called cementum covers it, although in most other mammals, this tissue is normally found only around the tooth’s root. Both materials contain collagen fibers reinforced with tiny mineral crystals, combining flexibility with hardness.

The arrangement works somewhat like reinforced concrete. In buildings, concrete withstands compression while a steel framework provides strength against pulling forces. In the narwhal’s tooth, collagen fibers serve as internal reinforcement, while mineral crystals provide hardness. “The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible,” Liebi explains. “Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.”.

The challenge for the researchers was finding out how these microscopic materials relate to the enormous spiral visible from the outside.

“The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths,” Liebi explains.

Recent findings suggest that to connect these vastly different scales, the team turned to a specialized X-ray technique called tensor tomography. Unlike an ordinary dental X-ray, which produces an image based on how strongly tissues absorb radiation, this method uses patterns created when powerful X-rays scatter from regularly arranged structures inside a material.

“From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented,” explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, who joined the project as a PhD student at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and later continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

Sources indicate that the researchers conducted their investigations at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at PSI in Villigen, Switzerland, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund, Sweden, and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in Grenoble, France. These facilities produce the powerful X-rays needed to examine extremely small structures.

Sources indicate that during tensor tomography, the tooth is rotated within the X-ray beam and scanned point by point. Millions of measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional picture of its internal architecture, connecting the orientation of nanoscale fibers with the structure of the entire tooth.

After collecting this enormous amount of data, however, the scientists encountered an unexpected problem. The spiral they were searching for appeared to be missing.

Sources indicate that “That puzzled us quite a bit,” Liebi recalls. Earlier mechanical tests had suggested that the tusk’s distinctive shape should already be reflected in the arrangement of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals. “But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.”.

It has been revealed that the answer emerged when the researchers changed how they examined the data. Rather than concentrating on individual points within the three-dimensional images, they began comparing how those points were oriented relative to one another.

In a recent development, “When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear,” recalls Rodriguez-Palomo. “All we had to do then was connect the dots – as in a children’s paint-by-numbers kit – and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.”.

The outer cementum layer followed a left-handed helix, while the mineralized collagen structures within the dentine twisted in the opposite direction. Together, these interlocking spirals create an unusually stable architecture, much like the twisted strands of a rope. Their opposing orientations help the tooth resist twisting forces and other mechanical stresses while contributing to its distinctive external spiral.

The researchers are also interested in another remarkable property of narwhal tusks: their ability to preserve a record of the Arctic environment.

Recent findings suggest that led by Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international team is investigating how tusk growth relates to environmental and climate conditions. Much like the annual rings of a tree, the growth structures within a narwhal’s tooth can provide clues about past conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

Because the tusk grows continuously, it can preserve environmental information across much of an animal’s life, which can approach a century. A tooth once mistaken for evidence of a mythical creature may therefore also hold a decades-long record of life in the Arctic.

Sources indicate that reference: “The narwhal tusk assembles its macroscopic helix from building blocks with opposing twists” by Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, Peter Alling Strange Vibe, Dimitra Athanasiadou, Jonas Palle, Leonard C. Nielsen, Jonathan T. Avaro, Thorbjørn Erik Køppen Christensen, Nina Kølln Wittig, Mads Ry Vogel Jørgensen, Innokenty Kantor, Manfred Burghammer, Jiliang Liu, Stefano Checchia, Christian Appel, Karl Anker Jørgensen, Eva Garde, Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen, Marianne Liebi and Henrik Birkedal, 18 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75689-z.

The study is part of the NordForsk-funded research project “Narwhal tusks – a tale with a twist.” It was supported by the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium.
  • In a recent development, the project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

In a recent development, these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have released the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

In a recent development, the project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

Industry observers note that first, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

Supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA.

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, mentioned in an HZDR statement:.

Sources indicate that this award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

To detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a newly introduced state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

Sources indicate that the results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," remarked Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub.".

His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. #31403. Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.
  • For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as crucial organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move.
  • In a recent development, coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.

For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as crucial organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move. Now, researchers at the University of Basel in Switzerland are revisiting that longstanding explanation, showing how scientific progress can sometimes begin by questioning what we thought we already knew.

In a recent development, coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans. They are involved in essential processes such as immunity, development, and cell survival. Scientists have traditionally viewed them as proteins that interact with actin, a major component of the cytoskeleton. This network of tiny filaments supports a cell’s structure, allows it to move, and helps organize its contents.

A new study published in PLOS Biology, led by Professor Jean Pieters at the University of Basel’s Biozentrum, challenges that understanding. Using a broad range of experiments to examine coronins in their natural state, the researchers found that these proteins are largely unnecessary for the overall organization of the actin cytoskeleton.

Sources indicate that “Over the years, my laboratory failed to find evidence for a direct role of coronin proteins in actin binding and modulation across a wide range of model systems,” states Pieters. “Even cells lacking coronins continue to organize and remodel their actin networks normally. Of course, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.”.

The team also identified a possible reason why earlier studies reached different conclusions. To observe proteins inside living cells, scientists often attach molecular tags that make them easier to track. Although these tools are widely used, they can sometimes interfere with the proteins being studied.

“These tags are extremely useful and assumed to be innocuous for protein function,” indicates Roko Gvozdenica, the study’s first author. “However, we found that the tagging of coronin proteins has the potential to cause loss of their function and significantly alter their localization.”.

This raises the possibility that some earlier evidence linking coronins to actin resulted from experimental artifacts rather than their natural behavior. The researchers also found that many antibodies used to detect coronins lack specificity, adding to broader concerns about the reliability of these tools in biomedical research.

The findings bring attention to another crucial role of coronins: helping cells communicate through chemical signals.

It has been revealed that “Over the years, we have reported that coronins are involved in cell signaling,” emphasizes Pieters. “In the immune system, for example, coronin involvement in these signaling processes was found to be essential for the maintenance of normal T cell numbers, which is vital for protecting the body against infections or cancer.”.

In a recent development, the researchers caution that their findings do not completely rule out a connection between coronins and the cytoskeleton. These proteins may still influence its organization, either directly or indirectly through cell signaling.

By reexamining an idea that has shaped research for decades, the study opens latest possibilities for understanding how coronins help cells communicate, survive, and maintain healthy cell numbers.

It has been revealed that reference: “Reassessment of the roles of coronin proteins as actin effectors and in signaling” by Roko Gvozdenica Šipić, Haiyan Zhang, Andrii Kharin, Jerneja Koren, Viviana D’Otolo, Yuko Nariai, Takeshi Urano, Pawel Pelczar, Klemens Fröhlich, Alexander Schmidt, Urszula Brykczynska Kunzmann, Tohnyui Ndinyanka Fabrice, Alexey Baldin and Jean Pieters, 18 August 2026, PLOS Biology. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003904.

#31402. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • Sources indicate that this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

Sources indicate that this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

Recent findings suggest that we update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Fresh to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Upcoming to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

It has been revealed that as Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“significant plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

It has been revealed that these days, London has no shortage of excellent upcoming-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

According to recent reports, this elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

According to recent reports, since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

Sources indicate that the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The upcoming online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

Recent findings suggest that there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Newly introduced York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

Sources indicate that after a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

In a recent development, clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

It has been revealed that while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most key British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

It has been revealed that given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Industry observers note that must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

According to recent reports, shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

According to recent reports, bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

According to recent reports, for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy latest surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Recent findings suggest that gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Industry observers note that mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a significant group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

In a recent development, A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

In a recent development, this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

It has been revealed that the second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Sources indicate that bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

The outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

Sources indicate that opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

Sources indicate that uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

The discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night.

According to recent reports, uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

The Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the new object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!).

According to recent reports, one of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson.

Can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only reveals a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Industry observers note that uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. Right now, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Challenge: Catching the Uranian Moons.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

Sources indicate that A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

The orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

In a recent development, the orbits of the moons are at the moment nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Sources indicate that hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

Scientists Solve a Longstanding Mystery About the Tiny Gateways That Protect Our DNA

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.
  • Every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored.
  • In a recent development, “As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most important molecular machines in the human cell,” said Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a new study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.

Every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored. Known as nuclear pores, these openings allow certain molecules to enter or leave while blocking others. Scientists have long understood the structure of these gateways, yet the proteins controlling what gets through have remained a mystery. Do they form a rigid barrier, or something more like a constantly shifting liquid?

In a recent development, “As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most important molecular machines in the human cell,” said Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a new study published in Nature. “And also one of the most complex,” added co-first author Maziar Heidari of the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany.

In a recent development, much of the uncertainty comes from how differently these proteins behave outside living cells. Previous experiments with isolated proteins produced everything from stretched chains to liquid-like droplets and thick gels resembling gummy bears. Some even formed solid deposits.

However, those observations could not establish what happens inside an actual nuclear pore, where thousands of molecular interactions help control traffic. “Such studies did not, however, allow any direct conclusions to be drawn about how the barrier behaves within the living cell,” said Professor Edward Lemke, Professor of Synthetic Biophysics at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU).

To investigate the barrier in its natural environment, Lemke and his colleagues attached fluorescent dyes to proteins inside the nuclear pores of living cells. These tiny glowing markers allowed the researchers to track protein movement and determine how flexible the barrier remained. The proteins moved rapidly throughout the entire two-hour observation period, indicating that the interior of the pore behaves more like a fluid than a solid.

“For the first time, we have been able to measure intrinsic protein dynamics within the nanocanal of a living cell and demonstrate that the interior of this canal is fluid-like,” noted Lemke, who led the study alongside Professor Gerhard Hummer of MPI-BP. “As the dyes move extremely swiftly, the state inside the nuclear pores must be fluid-like,” he explained.

The contrast became clearer when the researchers compared their observations with proteins isolated in a test tube. After approximately two hours, the protein material consistently hardened into a gummy-bear-like gel or an even more rigid solid. Some of these deposits resembled protein accumulations associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Inside living cells, however, the barrier remained flexible over the same period. “This was a crucial turning point: there had to be something keeping the barrier in the cells dynamic,” noted Lemke.

The researchers identified two components that helped explain the difference. One was a transport receptor, a protein involved in moving molecules through nuclear pores. The other was glycosylation, a process that attaches sugar groups to proteins and helps prevent them from sticking together too tightly. When both were included in the laboratory model, the proteins regained much of the mobility observed in living cells. “When we add these two components, we observe a similar mobility in the model system to that found in the nuclear pores of living cells,” said Lemke.

Recent findings suggest that understanding the barrier’s flexibility also helped the team tackle another longstanding puzzle: where molecules actually travel as they pass through the pore. In an ordinary pipe or river, flow is generally fastest near the center and slower along the edges. Earlier research suggested that nuclear pores work differently, with much of the transport occurring near their outer walls. One proposed explanation was that a biological structure, possibly a plug, occupied the middle and forced molecules toward the sides.

Recent findings suggest that hummer’s team investigated this possibility using what the researchers describe as the most comprehensive simulation model of a nuclear pore developed to date. The model incorporated experimental measurements from the Mainz team, including how extensively the barrier proteins were linked to one another. It allowed the researchers to examine how molecules would move through a pore with the physical properties they had measured.

“The simulations confirm that the main transport route runs along the edge of the pore,” stated Hummer. Importantly, the calculations revealed that this pattern could emerge from the pore’s physical and chemical properties without requiring a central obstruction. “While we do not rule out a biological cause such as a plug, it is not necessary from a physicochemical point of view.”.

Producing such a detailed model required enormous computing power. “These complex calculations were made possible by JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer at the Jülich Research Center,” remarked Hummer.

Sources indicate that the experiments and simulations provide a clearer picture of how nuclear pores maintain a flexible barrier while regulating the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus. They may also help researchers investigate why proteins that normally remain flexible sometimes harden into deposits, a process involved in neurodegenerative diseases.

According to recent reports, reference: “Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores” by Miao Yu (于淼), Maziar Heidari, Karen Palacio-Rodriguez, Hao Ruan (阮浩), Sara Mingu, Yu Chen (陈宇), Xu-Zhuo Gou (缑绪卓), Pingkai Shen (沈平恺), Songzi Liu (刘松子), Si-Yu Chen (陈思宇), Alam Ahmad Hidayat, Mathis Bode, Mateusz Sikora, Ai-Hui Tang (唐爱辉), Gerhard Hummer and Edward A. Lemke, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0.
