What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that for the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients.
  • According to recent reports, kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that for the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

According to recent reports, kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up new versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, indicates Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

It has been revealed that in the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi claims. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most important is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Sources indicate that mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” claims Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”.

Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, states Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and consumers are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann indicates, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

When people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

Industry observers note that while 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

Industry observers note that what is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving people in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman says.

Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she notes. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Now, it’s a different story, Sethi says.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she states. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

According to recent reports, in July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman notes. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will quickly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she says. “I think it’s important to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”.

#31294. Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1280 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • Industry observers note that meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Industry observers note that meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

After release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin stated.

According to recent reports, A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

The team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

The release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

According to recent reports, A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

According to recent reports, the release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

In a recent development, two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

Some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Recent findings suggest that solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

None of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

The authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

Recent findings suggest that on the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

In a recent development, the animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

This balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

In a recent development, the burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

According to recent reports, the researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

Industry observers note that the tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

It has been revealed that twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

Sources indicate that every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

It has been revealed that two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira noted the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

According to recent reports, but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These new forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make mentioned equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

Sources indicate that in a new study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

Recent findings suggest that “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, said in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

According to recent reports, “This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin mentioned. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

Sources indicate that according to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

Sources indicate that “Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines currently offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

In a recent development, this newly introduced study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

“Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin said. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a big data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite images show how quickly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.
  • Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite images show how quickly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.

Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.

Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye. In satellite images from a few hours earlier, the eye was still forming.

The MODIS instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this scene at 4:53 p.m. Cook Islands time on November 16, 2026.

By then, Xavier’s strongest sustained winds were estimated at about 120 miles per hour.

The clouds would tighten around a storm that was still gaining strength.

A few days earlier, the system that became Xavier was a loose cluster of thunderstorms.

In microwave satellite images from November 14, its structure was hard to make out.

By late November 16, distinct rainbands curved around a well-defined eye.

A separate sequence from the GOES-18 weather satellite highlights the eye becoming easier to pick out over the course of hours.

The difference between those views comes down to what each instrument can see.

A daylight image like this one highlights sunlight reflected by clouds and the ocean.

High clouds can hide the circulation beneath them, making it difficult to tell where a developing storm is centered.

Microwave observations can reveal parts of the rain structure beneath those clouds, giving forecasters another way to follow a storm as it organizes.

It has been revealed that the eye is typically the calmest part of a mature tropical cyclone. Air sinks there, which helps keep clouds from forming.

Industry observers note that just outside it, warm, moist air rises in a ring of thunderstorms called the eyewall. That ring is usually where the storm’s strongest winds are found.

Farther from the center, the sweeping bands visible from space can bring bursts of heavy rain and wind, with quieter stretches in between.

Someone on an island can experience several rounds of rough weather as successive bands pass overhead, even when the eye stays out at sea.

In a recent development, from above, the bands look like parts of a single spiral. On the ground, they can feel like a series of separate storms.

It has been revealed that the ocean beneath Xavier was about 84 degrees Fahrenheit, warm enough to supply plenty of heat and moisture. Winds also changed relatively little with height.

That meant there was little wind shear to tilt the storm and push its thunderstorms away from the center, allowing them to build around the same developing circulation.

Xavier also formed near the southwestern edge of a broad stretch of unusually warm water associated with El Niño.

During El Niño years, cyclones in the Southwest Pacific tend to form farther toward the central Pacific, shifting where island communities are most likely to encounter them.

Xavier developed on the eastern side of the international date line, near the northern Cook Islands.

The storm eventually reached Category 5 on the scale used in the South Pacific. As it moved west, it encountered drier air and stronger wind shear and began to weaken.

On Manihiki, one of the northern Cook Islands, the rain kept falling after the winds began to ease.

A resident told Pacific Media Network that some homes had lost sections of corrugated roofing and that electricity remained a concern.

The island was relying on solar power after losing its main diesel generator more than a year earlier, and the storm’s persistent cloud cover made it harder to keep batteries charged.

Sources indicate that emergency generators helped residents keep essential supplies cold. The island had also begun preparing well before Xavier appeared on satellite maps.

Each October, the island council begins removing hazardous coconut trees near homes and roads, a practice shaped by the damage Cyclone Martin inflicted on the northern Cook Islands in 1997.

Aqua passed over Xavier once that afternoon, catching a brief moment when the storm’s eye was in clear view.

On Manihiki, one of the most consequential features of the storm was the cloud cover that lingered after the worst winds had passed.

The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.
  • Recent findings suggest that the highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 17, 2026 at 12:50 pm.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

Recent findings suggest that the highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO declared; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa remarked in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

According to recent reports, measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

Recent findings suggest that “To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo mentioned. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”.

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

According to recent reports, the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, claims Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and promptly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”.

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

According to recent reports, A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, remarked in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”.

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”.

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health.

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

Sources indicate that homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States highlighted that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, states Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

According to recent reports, measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento notes. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer mentioned in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive strategy at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in latest states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo states. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

In a recent development, there’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo indicates. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has mentioned the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”.

Sources indicate that eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo claims. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”.

Industry observers note that public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo remarked. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”.

Meet the Planimal: Half Hamster Cell, Half Algae, 100% Weird

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception.
  • Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.

Obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their newly introduced study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

“We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, stated in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”.

To investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

In a recent development, “Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga said. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”.

Sources indicate that the key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”.

In a recent development, “Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”.

Sources indicate that darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#31288. When should women start thinking about heart disease? Earlier than you might expect

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1263 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

When should women start thinking about heart disease? Earlier than you might expect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.
  • Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.
  • Yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.

Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.

Yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S. than breast cancer and lung cancer combined, and much of what sets a woman’s risk happens decades before menopause.

New joint guidance from four medical societies tells doctors to start reading that risk at a girl’s first period.

The guidance comes as three papers from the American Heart Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

It’s built from existing evidence rather than a new trial, so it reorganizes what doctors already know instead of adding a new finding.

It has been revealed that sadiya Khan, a cardiologist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, chaired the writing group. In an interview with Earth.com, she compared it to saving money.

According to recent reports, “You would never wait until retirement to start saving. We should bring that same thinking to heart health,” Khan remarked.

Standard cardiovascular risk calculators already account for sex, but they don’t capture every risk factor tied to a woman’s reproductive history.

Industry observers note that the upcoming framework splits a woman’s life into four stages set by her hormones. They are the years around the first period, the decades of regular cycles, the transition into menopause, and the years after it.

Pregnancy counts as a separate event, running from 12 months before conception to 12 months after delivery.

Estrogen and progesterone act on blood vessels, heart muscle and the brain, not only on the reproductive organs.

Because those hormones rise and fall about once a month, with no equivalent in men, blood vessel function and sleep vary in the same rhythm.

The authors wrote that risk in each stage is shaped by the stages before it.

Asked by Earth.com which stage is most overlooked, Khan said the biggest gaps are what happened earlier, such as irregular or heavy periods, pregnancy complications and a diagnosis like endometriosis.

Those shape heart health in later stages, she said, and belong in the conversation at every visit.

Recent findings suggest that “Heart health for women doesn’t start at menopause,” stated Amanda Perak, a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago who worked on all three papers. “Puberty is a big turning point.”.

A first period before age 10 is linked to higher heart disease risk later in life, and the 2026 cholesterol guideline already lists it as a risk enhancer.

Sources indicate that some irregularity is normal in the first one to three years. A pattern that persists can signal the hormone disorder that used to be called polycystic ovary syndrome, which often comes with insulin resistance and unhealthy cholesterol.

The disorder, now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, affects an estimated 10% to 13% of women.

In a recent development, heavy periods affect 20% to 30% of young women, and about half of those with heavy bleeding are low on iron. The authors wrote that menstrual patterns may be the earliest sign of heart risk a doctor can see.

Sources indicate that mental health turns in the same years. By about age 17, girls have at least twice the odds of a depression diagnosis as boys.

Industry observers note that teens with depression are more likely to develop obesity later, and the reverse holds too. Nearly one in five girls in organized sports consider quitting over menstrual concerns, the authors wrote.

“The goal isn’t to worry teens about the chance of a heart attack, which are decades away for nearly all of them,” Perak stated.

“It’s that the teen years are when patterns get set, and it’s much easier to keep good heart health than to get it back.”.

Estrogen levels in pregnancy rise to about 30 times their peak in a normal cycle, and the heart and metabolism both change to support the fetus.

The authors call it a stress test because it can expose risk that was already there.

Nearly nine in ten women ages 20 to 44 begin pregnancy with less-than-ideal heart health.

High blood pressure in pregnancy, gestational diabetes and preterm birth are each linked to higher heart disease risk later in life.

Mood and anxiety disorders affect up to 37% of women in the first three months after delivery.

The year after a birth is a vulnerable time for follow-up. Women move from obstetric care back to primary care, and that handoff is often missed.

The guidance notes that the obstetric threshold for hypertension, a systolic reading of at least 140 or a diastolic reading of at least 90, matches the cutoff for stage 2 hypertension in general adult care.

Perimenopause begins at a median age of about 47 in the U.S., and the authors describe it as a period of swings rather than a steady decline.

LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol, rises during the transition independent of aging. Hot flashes affect 50% to 80% of women in this stage, and about one in three report significant depression or anxiety symptoms.

In a recent development, women then spend about 40% of their lives after menopause. Around 67 million American women are 50 or older, and an estimated 6,000 more reach menopause every day.

Menopause that arrives early carries extra heart risk of its own.

Hormone therapy can help manage menopause symptoms, but the authors advise against using it to prevent heart disease.

In a recent development, years of unhealthy habits may begin to show in this stage as heart disease. Stacey Rosen, the association’s immediate past volunteer president, remarked it is never too late to do something about it.

“It’s always about opportunities,” Rosen said.

A woman may see a pediatrician, a primary care doctor, an obstetrician, a cardiologist and a psychologist over her life, and their notes rarely travel with her.

One of the three papers surveyed 70 leaders of women’s cardiovascular centers and heard back from 33.

Of those programs, 29 are in cities and one is rural, and the paper proposes a national network of centers that combine the specialties.

Khan told Earth.com the papers are a first step toward giving every clinician the same playbook.

The next change, she said, is connecting all the clinicians on a woman’s care team through the life stage framework.

Industry observers note that her advice for the next appointment was a single question. “Ask at every life stage: What is my heart risk, and what should I do about it now? It is never too early to talk about your heart health,” she mentioned.

The framework rests on evidence that links these stages to risk, and the papers say plainly where the links are weakest.

In a recent development, it isn’t known whether treating severe hot flashes lowers heart disease risk, with or without hormones. Female-specific cutoffs for heart imaging tests aren’t yet in guidelines.

And none of the three papers reports a trial showing that sorting care by life stage, rather than by age, prevents more heart attacks and strokes.

Khan mentioned she is especially interested in reaching younger women now that risk can be estimated up to 30 years ahead with the association’s PREVENT equations.

Whether clinics can be rebuilt around that forecast is the test the four societies have set themselves.

The research was published in the journal Circulation.

#31286. Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (961 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.
  • The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.
  • Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.

The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.

Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.

Chemical traces in fossil shells suggest that microscopic plants at the ocean’s surface used a smaller share of the nutrients available to them than they did in cooler periods before and after.

That left more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, according to the study’s model.

The model suggests that the weaker carbon pump and the feedbacks it amplified could explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide at the time.

In a recent development, simone Moretti of the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz, Germany, led the study. His co-authors came from the Université libre de Bruxelles (ULB), the University of California, Santa Cruz and other institutions.

“Our study shows that the Southern Ocean played a major role in regulating atmospheric CO2 during the early Eocene, millions of years before the onset of the recent ice ages,” Moretti said.

It has been revealed that the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum ran from about 53 to 49 million years ago. Global temperatures were more than 18°F (10°C) higher than now, and carbon dioxide reached around 1,600 parts per million.

The causes of those levels are still debated. Volcanoes and reduced burial of organic carbon have both been proposed, but the timing of the eruptions lines up poorly with the warming.

According to recent reports, so the team looked at the ocean’s biological carbon pump. Microscopic plants near the surface take up carbon dioxide as they grow. When they die, some of that carbon sinks and stays in the deep ocean for hundreds to thousands of years.

Today the pump runs below its full potential. Deep water rising around Antarctica brings up nutrients that the plants never fully use.

Plankton prefer the lighter form of nitrogen when they take up nitrate, their main nutrient. The more completely they use the supply, the heavier the leftover nitrogen becomes.

The nitrogen signature ends up in the shells of foraminifera, single-celled organisms that eat the plankton. The team measured the nitrogen trapped in fossil foraminifera from four sediment cores drilled by the Ocean Drilling Program.

Two cores came from the Southern Ocean. Two came from the mid-latitude Atlantic and Indian oceans, where nutrients are used up almost completely.

The gap between the two pairs of sites shows how much nutrient the Southern Ocean plants left behind. It was widest exactly when temperatures and carbon dioxide peaked, and it narrowed or vanished before and after.

The team then ran a simple model of the ocean and atmosphere using the estimated 40% drop in the share of available nutrients that plankton used.

On its own, the drop raised carbon dioxide from 700 to about 900 parts per million.

When the researchers included the effects of warming and changes in seawater chemistry, atmospheric carbon dioxide reached about 1,100 parts per million.

That increase accounts for about half of the roughly 800 parts per million rise reconstructed for the period.

In a recent development, the leak hit harder than it would today. Eocene seawater was more acidic and richer in calcium, so it had less capacity to absorb a change in carbon dioxide.

“Because Eocene seawater had a much lower capacity to buffer changes in CO2 than today’s ocean, a weakening of the biological carbon pump could have had a far greater impact on atmospheric CO2 than under present-day conditions,” said François Fripiat, a co-author at ULB.

Over millions of years, rain and rock weathering normally pull carbon dioxide back out of the air and act as a thermostat.

The early Eocene had no Alps or Himalayas yet, and its flat, deeply weathered continents offered little fresh rock.

“With Earth’s natural thermostat operating less efficiently, the additional CO2 released from the ocean could remain in the atmosphere for much longer,” said Mathis Hain, a co-author at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“This would allow the Southern Ocean to influence climate not just over thousands of years, as during the ice ages, but over millions of years,” he noted.

The Southern Ocean also released carbon dioxide during warm spells between recent ice ages.

The authors interpret the match across very different timescales as a sign of a dependable feedback.

Sources indicate that the shells record that the plants left nutrients unused, but not why. Stronger mixing around Antarctica could have brought up more deep water, or the plants could have grown less.

In a recent development, the authors argued that iron supply, which limits plant growth there today, likely changed little in a warmer world. That leaves less room for the growth explanation.

The estimate of the nutrient drop is deliberately conservative, because one of the mid-latitude sites falls between the others in its values.

And the carbon model is a simple one, built to show the size of the effect rather than reproduce the Eocene ocean.

The open question is whether the modern Southern Ocean will respond the same way.

Simulations run for centuries to thousands of years suggest deep-water formation near Antarctica strengthens once the deep ocean catches up with surface warming, which would match the Eocene pattern.

The team is now exploring the same feedback in other periods of sustained warming. The paper names the Middle Eocene, the Middle Miocene and the Pliocene as candidates.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#31285. What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.
  • In a recent development, A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk.
  • Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.

In a recent development, A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk. Could a computer start from scratch and recognize many of those same words on roughly the same timetable?

Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.

The researchers turned speech recorded around eight children into clean audio using synthetic voices.

They trained a separate model on each child’s audio in the order the speech was originally recorded.

The models identified recurring sound patterns that corresponded to words.

On average, each model reached the halfway point on a vocabulary checklist within 22 days of the child it was paired with.

“We wanted to turn the usual logic of developmental research around,” remarked Uri Hasson, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Princeton who led the study.

“Instead of observing a child for an hour in the laboratory, we asked whether we could build a model capable of learning and immerse it in the child’s actual experience, day after day.”.

It has been revealed that the families were in Fresh Jersey and spanned a range of incomes and backgrounds. Each home got four to 14 recording devices spread across two to five rooms.

The devices ran 12 to 14 hours a day, from February 2022 to May 2025.

The project gathered roughly 1.2 million hours of audio and video, of which the eight homes analyzed in this paper supplied about 600,000. An automated pipeline worked out where the child was in the house and pulled out the speech happening nearby.

Sources indicate that each child ended up with between 1,900 and 6,600 hours of usable speech, three to seven and a half hours a day. That adds up to 6 to 27 million words per child, over a median of 960 recording days.

Sources indicate that every month from eight months on, caregivers filled out a standard checklist of which words their child understood and noted. Those forms are how the researchers knew what each child knew, and when.

Sources indicate that children reached half of the 649-word checklist anywhere from about 12 to 22 months old. That ten-month spread between children is the thing most studies average away.

The model started from random numbers. It had no dictionary, no phonetics, no notion of where one word ends and the next begins, and no text.

Industry observers note that the program’s first part chops the incoming sound into 20-millisecond pieces and sorts them into categories it invents for itself. Its second part tries to guess the next piece from what came before.

Whenever a run of pieces becomes reliably predictable, the program files it away as a unit, which is the closest thing it has to a word.

Nothing about that design is specific to English or even to speech. What makes it unusual is the schedule.

The audio arrives in the order it was recorded, one day at a time, rather than shuffled into batches the way an AI language model is normally trained.

Industry observers note that at the end of each simulated day, the program gets a sample of speech from earlier days, weighted toward recent ones. The researchers call it replay.

According to recent reports, english has 39 phonemes, the sound units that distinguish bat from pat. Children spend their first year tuning in to the ones their own language uses.

Within roughly 12 to 15 months of simulated time, the program had carved out dedicated categories for nearly all of them.

Industry observers note that across the eight children, the models averaged 37.5 phonemes each. The lowest count came from the household with the least recording.

The order it happened in, sounds before words, is the order infants follow.

According to recent reports, words came after. For the child the paper calls Coral, the checklist said she understood 97 words at 12 months, and her model had 91.

Across all eight children, the models and the children hit the same vocabulary milestones within an average of 22 days of each other, with the worst case 56 days.

The models also reproduced the differences between children, landing close to each child’s own halfway age.

They did not match perfectly. The models tended to start learning words a little late and then catch up faster, so the shape of the curve was only partly right.

The surprise in the paper is what happened when the researchers took replay away.

It has been revealed that coral’s household produced something like 10 million words a year, which is a rich environment by any measure. Hearing all of it once, in order, wasn’t enough. With a single pass the program barely learned words at all.

Around 25 to 30 passes over each day’s material was enough, and more than that added very little.

The researchers link this to what sleep is thought to do for memory. A program replaying audio files is not a sleeping infant, and the paper is careful about that.

The amount of recording mattered just as much. Fed only a tenth of Coral’s daily speech, under an hour a day, the program learned none of the checklist words by 24 months.

At 30% of the day, about two and a half hours, it learned 80 of the 649 checklist words.

At 70% it got about nine-tenths of the way to the full result. The rarer words, it seems, only turn up for a listener who is there most of the day.

Sources indicate that one limitation shapes everything else. Household recordings are full of clattering dishes, television, and two people talking at once, and the program was not asked to cope with any of that.

Instead the researchers transcribed all the speech around each child, then had a text-to-speech system read the transcripts back as clean audio.

Each household got a mix of eight adult female voices, with 30% of segments read in a voice matched to the child’s mother.

Industry observers note that so the word order, the timing and the vocabulary are real, and the sound isn’t. The acoustic problem a baby actually solves, picking one voice out of a noisy room, was left for later work.

Three of the eight children also had shorter recordings, 14 to 20 months of usable input, so their later trajectories are extrapolated rather than modeled.

The program also sees nothing: no faces, no pointing, no object being handed over, which is a large part of how toddlers work out what a word refers to.

The program learned sounds and words. It did not learn grammar, and whether the same machinery would arrive at sentence structure is the open question the authors name.

In a recent development, the team wants to use the setup for questions nobody can put to a real baby. What would less sleep do, or screen speech instead of a parent’s?

Future studies could also add eye contact and the rest of the social world the cameras captured but the model never saw.

Hadas Raviv, a computational cognitive scientist in Princeton’s psychology department who built the analysis pipeline, framed the goal as the opposite of the usual one in artificial intelligence.

“Unlike much of modern AI, which aims for superhuman performance, we’re trying to understand how humans learn and how that learning gives rise to intelligence,” Raviv said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#31282. A dead star sends out radio signals every eight minutes, then goes quiet for a day

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1032 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A dead star sends out radio signals every eight minutes, then goes quiet for a day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A white dwarf beside a Sun-like star sends out radio pulses every 7.9 minutes, the first of its kind found with such a companion.
  • Recent findings suggest that when a star like the Sun dies, it leaves behind a dense core called a white dwarf.
  • It’s the first known radio-pulsing white dwarf with a Sun-like companion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A white dwarf beside a Sun-like star sends out radio pulses every 7.9 minutes, the first of its kind found with such a companion.

Recent findings suggest that when a star like the Sun dies, it leaves behind a dense core called a white dwarf. Astronomers found one that sends out a burst of radio waves every 7.9 minutes during a roughly six-hour window.

It’s the first known radio-pulsing white dwarf with a Sun-like companion.

Radio-pulsing white dwarfs have been seen before, but every one with a known partner had a small, dim red dwarf beside it.

Small shifts in when the pulses arrive revealed the radio source moving with the white dwarf. That places the source on or near the star itself.

Sam McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist at the SKA Observatory, led the work.

The research was conducted at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research in Western Australia, with six colleagues in Australia, Spain, the United States, and Britain.

In an interview with Earth.com, co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker was asked what surprised her most when the team saw the white dwarf moving.

“We were extremely excited!” she noted. “We knew immediately that this would be an independent test of our hypothesis that it was the orbital geometry that was causing the radio waves to appear and disappear every 32.5 hours.”.

The source turned up in a survey of the Milky Way with the Murchison Widefield Array, a field of radio antennas in the Western Australian outback.

On December 4, 2024, it produced a run of bright pulses, each under four seconds long and spaced 7.9 minutes apart.

Recent findings suggest that over the next nine months, the array caught 214 of them. The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa added 33 and fixed the position precisely enough to match it to a star in the Gaia catalog.

Spectra from the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii indicated that star to be a G-type star. Its surface is near 9,400°F (5,200°C), and it has about 94% of the Sun’s mass.

The system, cataloged as GPM J071507−114153, is roughly 11,000 light-years away, with a wide margin of error.

A pulse every 7.9 minutes is too fast for an ordinary star to spin without flying apart. So the pulsing object has to be something compact: a white dwarf or a neutron star.

Many follow-up observations caught nothing at the predicted times.

When the team sorted the hits and misses, a second rhythm appeared. The pulses are only on for about six hours, and that window comes around every 32.5 hours.

The team interprets the 32.5-hour cycle as the orbital period and the 7.9-minute spacing as the white dwarf’s spin period.

The researchers think the stars’ positions in their orbit determine when the pulses reach Earth.

In a recent development, the timing gave them more. If the radio source orbits with the white dwarf, its distance to Earth changes as it goes around. Its pulses should then arrive a few seconds early on one side of the orbit and late on the other. They did.

Industry observers note that hurley-Walker said that delay is what let the team say where in the orbit the waves are made. Without it, she said, they could have been coming from the pair’s common center of mass, which doesn’t move.

The companion’s spectrum shows it swinging at no more than about 110,000 miles per hour (50 kilometers per second). Combined with the delay, that caps the mass of the compact object.

The cap is too low for a neutron star, so the team settled on a white dwarf.

Sources indicate that astronomers call these objects long-period transients, radio sources that switch on and off over minutes to hours. The first one was found in 2021. The paper counts a dozen, four of them confirmed as a white dwarf paired with a red dwarf.

Theorists built their models for how the pulses arise on that pairing, with the red dwarf’s wind and magnetic field feeding the white dwarf.

A G-type companion in a 1.3-day orbit is a counterexample, and the authors wrote that the models will need to stretch to include it.

In a recent development, hurley-Walker noted the find also opens a different door. A Sun-like star outshines a white dwarf in visible light, so pairs like this one are hard for optical telescopes to pick out.

“Radio telescopes can now find these binaries that optical telescopes would have struggled to detect, which gives astronomers a fresh window on understanding binary systems,” she told Earth.com.

The MeerKAT pulses carried another clue. The orientation of the radio waves, known as their polarization, rotated the most when the white dwarf passed behind its companion.

That can happen when radio waves pass through magnetized gas. The pattern resembles what spacecraft have measured near the Sun’s corona.

“What we think is happening is that the radio waves from the white dwarf are passing through the magnetic field of its stellar companion,” Hurley-Walker remarked.

According to recent reports, the authors left a second explanation open. A mass ejection from the companion could have crossed the line of sight by chance, since only 14 pulses had a usable twist measurement.

How the white dwarf makes the pulses is still unknown. The team has almost no handle on its magnetic field, and the distance to the system is uncertain by thousands of light-years.

The two arrays that found it are both forerunners of the Square Kilometre Array, now being built in Australia and South Africa, and McSweeney is helping commission the Australian half.

Hurley-Walker said she is designing surveys for it to find more of these systems and to test where they are, how fast they pulse, and how bright they get.

The detection software that found this one, she added, was written by Curtin doctoral student Csanád Horváth.

Until those surveys run, this eight-minute pulse beside a Sun-like star is a single system, and the modelers have to explain it.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.
